newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral to be sworn in as prime minister.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral to be sworn in as prime minister.

text.p: Inder Kumar Gujral, a scholarly 77-year-old, will be sworn in on Monday as India's fourth prime minister in a turbulent political year in the world's biggest democracy.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma was due to administer the oath of office to Gujral, foreign minister in the outgoing United Front government, at 10 a.m. (0430 GMT) in the ornate sandstone presidential palace.
Gujral's appointment followed three weeks of political upheaval triggered by the Congress party's shock decision last month to withdraw vital support to the 10-month-old centre-left government.

But after Sharma asked Gujral to form a new government, question marks lingered over the intentions of a powerful regional constituent of the ruling coalition and the future of the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March).

A United Front spokesman said outgoing Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, one of the architects of India's economic liberalisation programme and the author of the pathbreaking budget, was certain to retain his job.

But Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress party, piqued at being passed over during wrangling over a successor to caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, vowed to pull out of the government while still supporting it in parliament.
A senior United Front official said the coalition was confident of succeeding in mollifying its sulking constituent before the new cabinet was sworn in on Monday.

The Tamil party's tantrum was only one of the problems facing Gujral in piecing together a cabinet to satisfy the 15 disparate parties of the United Front, which loosely groups socialists, communists, regional parties and free traders.
But the United Front official said it was certain that Chidambaram would shepherd his budget proposals through parliament by the end of the month.
With the help of the 140 Congress votes, the United Front's 178 deputies should easily push the budget through the 542-member lower house of parliament.
Congress support to the nascent government will also be crucial on Tuesday, when Gujral will have to show that he has the backing of a majority of members in the hung parliament.
The United Front and Congress are united perhaps only in their opposition to the largest single party, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, which has 194 seats.
